## Guided Tutorial 11.2: Tracking the Gap Month by Month

**Context and objective.** In Chapter 10 you followed the conversion cost through account 1090 for whole years. In this tutorial, you will measure the gap between the actual cost charged to the account and the standard cost released by completions for each month, accumulate it through each year, compare each month with the same month a year earlier, and rank the months. You will then rank the work centers by the hours recorded against their planned hours.

**Prerequisites.** Complete Tutorial 11.1, and continue in Chapter11.sql.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Calculate the monthly gap and its year-to-date total.** The payroll and journal entries debit account 1090 with actual cost, and completions credit it with standard cost. The work order closes, which clear the difference, are left out.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod,
       ROUND(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit), 2) AS Gap,
       ROUND(SUM(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit)) OVER (
           PARTITION BY FiscalYear ORDER BY FiscalPeriod), 2) AS GapYearToDate
   FROM GLEntry
   WHERE AccountID = 92 AND FiscalYear BETWEEN 2024 AND 2026
       AND SourceDocumentType <> 'WorkOrderClose'
   GROUP BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod
   ORDER BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod;
   ```

b. Read the GapYearToDate column in the December row of each year.

The result, shown in @fig-11-04, has one row for each month. The window function sums the monthly gaps within each fiscal year, in order of period, and starts again at zero each January. The December figure is the year's total gap, and it grew in each year: by fiscal 2026 it was nearly twice the figure of fiscal 2024. The window works on the results of the grouping, because window functions are calculated after GROUP BY.

![The Monthly Gap in Account 1090 and Its Year-to-Date Total.](/visuals/svg/fig-11-04-gap-year-to-date.svg){#fig-11-04 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL tab. The query groups the postings to account 1090, without the work order closes, by fiscal year and period, and calculates the monthly gap between actual and standard cost and a year-to-date total with SUM over a window partitioned by fiscal year. The grid shows the twelve months of fiscal 2026, and the GapYearToDate column, which accumulates through the year, is outlined."}

**Step 2. Compare each month with the same month a year earlier.** LAG with an offset of 12 reaches back twelve rows, one year of months.

a. Add a column after GapYearToDate, so that the query reads as below, and run it.

   ```sql
   SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod,
       ROUND(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit), 2) AS Gap,
       ROUND(SUM(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit)) OVER (
           PARTITION BY FiscalYear ORDER BY FiscalPeriod), 2) AS GapYearToDate,
       ROUND(LAG(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit), 12) OVER (
           ORDER BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod), 2) AS GapSameMonthLastYear
   FROM GLEntry
   WHERE AccountID = 92 AND FiscalYear BETWEEN 2024 AND 2026
       AND SourceDocumentType <> 'WorkOrderClose'
   GROUP BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod
   ORDER BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod;
   ```

b. Compare the Gap and GapSameMonthLastYear columns for the months of fiscal 2026.

The LAG column is NULL for the twelve months of fiscal 2024, which have no earlier year in the data. In most months of fiscal 2026, the gap was larger than in the same month of fiscal 2025. The comparison with the same month removes the effect of the season, which a comparison with the previous month would not.

**Step 3. Rank the months within each year.** A ranking function numbers the months by the size of their gap, and a derived table lets the outer query keep the top three of each year.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod, Gap, GapRank
   FROM (
       SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod,
           ROUND(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit), 2) AS Gap,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY FiscalYear
               ORDER BY SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit) DESC) AS GapRank
       FROM GLEntry
       WHERE AccountID = 92 AND FiscalYear BETWEEN 2024 AND 2026
           AND SourceDocumentType <> 'WorkOrderClose'
       GROUP BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod
   ) AS monthly
   WHERE GapRank <= 3
   ORDER BY FiscalYear, GapRank;
   ```

b. Read the three largest months of each year.

The query returns nine rows, three for each year. The ranking cannot be filtered in the inner query's WHERE clause, because WHERE runs before the window function is calculated. The derived table calculates the rank first, and the outer WHERE keeps the top three. In each year, the largest months are two or more times the size of the smallest ones, a reminder of how much a single month can swing.

**Step 4. Rank the work centers by the hours recorded against their plan.** Each work order operation records its planned hours and its work center, and the direct labor time is recorded against the operation.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   SELECT CloseYear, WorkCenterName, PlannedHours, RecordedHours,
       ROUND(RecordedHours / PlannedHours, 2) AS RecordedPerPlanned,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY CloseYear
           ORDER BY RecordedHours / PlannedHours DESC) AS CenterRank
   FROM (
       SELECT strftime('%Y', op.ActualEndDate) AS CloseYear,
           wc.WorkCenterName,
           ROUND(SUM(op.PlannedLoadHours), 0) AS PlannedHours,
           ROUND(SUM(lab.Hours), 0) AS RecordedHours
       FROM WorkOrderOperation AS op
           INNER JOIN WorkCenter AS wc ON wc.WorkCenterID = op.WorkCenterID
           LEFT JOIN (
               SELECT WorkOrderOperationID,
                   SUM(RegularHours + OvertimeHours) AS Hours
               FROM LaborTimeEntry
               WHERE LaborType = 'Direct Manufacturing'
               GROUP BY WorkOrderOperationID
           ) AS lab ON lab.WorkOrderOperationID = op.WorkOrderOperationID
       WHERE op.ActualEndDate IS NOT NULL
       GROUP BY CloseYear, wc.WorkCenterName
   ) AS centers
   ORDER BY CloseYear, CenterRank;
   ```

b. Compare the RecordedPerPlanned column across the work centers and years.

The result, shown in @fig-11-05, ranks the five work centers within each year. The pattern is lopsided. Packing and Quality Assurance record far more direct hours than their operations planned, several times more by fiscal 2026, while Assembly, Cutting, and Finishing record well under their plans, and the gap widens in each year. An efficiency problem would be expected to show up across the plant. Hours concentrated at the end of the routing, beyond anything planned there, could instead mean that time is being recorded against the wrong operations. That is a finding to investigate, not yet an explanation.

![Work Centers Ranked by Hours Recorded Against Plan.](/visuals/svg/fig-11-05-work-center-rank.svg){#fig-11-05 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL tab. The query compares the direct labor hours recorded against each work center's operations with their planned load hours, by year, and ranks the work centers with RANK over a window partitioned by year. The grid shows fifteen rows, five work centers for each of three years. Packing and Quality Assurance rank first and second in each year with several times their planned hours, and those rows are outlined."}

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- the year-to-date gap restarts each January, and its December figure grew in each year;
- the same-month comparison is NULL for fiscal 2024 and shows larger gaps in most months of fiscal 2026;
- the ranking query returns the three largest months of each year, filtered in the outer query;
- Packing and Quality Assurance record several times their planned hours, while the other work centers record less than planned.

The window functions show that the gap grew steadily and was not the work of a few bad months. They also expose a pattern in the time records that the controller cannot explain from the numbers alone.
